title: The Courtauld Gallery: Masterpieces
subtitle: Twenty works that make looking, reflection and unequal awareness part of the subject.
introduction:
The barmaid stands close to the spectator, yet the mirror behind her makes that apparently direct encounter difficult to locate. In another painting, a watcher leans over a sleeping figure; in a landscape, travellers nearly disappear into the terrain they must cross. The Courtauld selection repeatedly changes who has access to a scene and how much they can know about it.

That question extends to the objects themselves. A drawing of the Colossus reconstructs a lost monument without becoming evidence of its original appearance. A study for a dance isolates movements rather than recording a complete performance. Looking requires attention to the kind of image in front of us as well as its subject.
visitNote: This selection includes paintings and works on paper from the Courtauld collection. Drawings and watercolours rotate for conservation, and individual works may be on loan. Check the gallery’s current display information before expecting to see all twenty in one visit.

books.title: Impressionism: A Centenary Exhibition
books.author: Anne Dayez, Michel Hoog and Charles S. Moffett
books.note: The exhibition catalogue places Manet, Seurat and the painters around them within the debates of nineteenth-century art. Its illustrations support comparisons of public entertainment, private interiors and the changing marks used to describe them.

works.title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
works.credit: Édouard Manet. A Bar at the Folies-Bergère. Image credit: Édouard Manet; Source credit: Un bar aux Folies-Bergère d'E. Manet (Fondation Vuitton, Paris); Photograph: Jean-Pierre Dalbéra (https://www.flickr.com/people/72746018@N00), explicitly credited in the Commons file Author field.. CC BY 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: The counter offers a close, apparently secure position in front of the barmaid. Her reflection, shifted to the right, unsettles it. The Courtauld identifies the sitter as Suzon, who posed in Manet’s studio after he made on-site sketches. The finished picture is a constructed encounter, not a transparent snapshot of the music hall.

works.title: Nevermore
works.credit: Paul Gauguin. Nevermore. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The reclining woman turns her head toward a room containing other figures and a bird. The painted title adds another sign without settling the relations among them. Gauguin’s setting should not be read as straightforward documentation of Tahitian life. Its watchers and conversations belong to an image whose arrangement keeps their meaning uncertain.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
works.credit: Vincent van Gogh. Self Portrait with Bandaged Ear. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The bandage is conspicuous, but it is not the portrait’s only information. Coat, cap, studio setting and the print behind the figure remain present through firm contours and differentiated strokes. Van Gogh’s injury belongs within a continuing act of representation. Biography can identify the condition without accounting for every pictorial choice.

works.title: Young Woman Powdering Herself
works.credit: Georges Seurat. Young Woman Powdering Herself. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The powder puff brings the hand near the face and gives the seated pose a practical purpose. Rounded forms repeat through hair, arm, bodice and dressing table. Across them, divided marks of colour maintain their own surface. A private routine becomes recognisable through both an action and a carefully related arrangement of curves.

works.title: Study for Le Chahut
works.credit: Georges Seurat. Study for The Chahut. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The raised leg and neighbouring curved form establish a dance through repeated directions. This is a study, so its narrow selection need not explain an entire performance. The marks test how coordinated movement can remain legible when the individual performer is reduced to a part within a larger pattern.

works.title: Landscape with the Flight into Egypt
works.catalogueTitle: Landscape with the Flight into Egypt
works.credit: Pieter Bruegel the Elder. Landscape with the Flight into Egypt. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/pieter-bruegel-the-elder/landscape-with-the-flight-into-egypt-1563
works.description: The travellers are small beside the river, mountains and settlements. Their route has to be found within a view that can first appear available simply as an extensive landscape. Once recognised, the group changes the scale of attention: this large world is also ground through which vulnerable people must make their way.

works.title: The Dream of Human Life
works.credit: The Dream of Human Life. WikiArt; Michelangelo. Proportional resizing and JPEG compression; source frame preserved.
works.description: The central nude has a solidity that the smaller surrounding scenes do not share. A winged figure approaches above, while masks and other images complicate the apparently self-contained body. The drawing brings the person into relation with roles and visions around him, without turning those relations into one continuous everyday setting.

works.title: The Conversion of Saint Paul
works.credit: Peter Paul Rubens. Conversion of Saint Paul. Image credit: Peter Paul Rubens. Wikimedia Commons. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Resized and JPEG-compressed; selected source frame preserved.
works.description: Riders and horses lose their coordinated movement as light enters the crowded scene. Falling bodies and opposed directions make conversion visible as an interruption of control. Rubens gives the event a physical consequence before every figure is distinguished: the group’s previous order can no longer hold.

works.title: The Coronation of the Virgin
works.credit: Peter Paul Rubens. Coronation of the Virgin. Image credit: Peter Paul Rubens. Wikimedia Commons. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Resized and JPEG-compressed; selected source frame preserved.
works.description: Mary’s kneeling position remains identifiable amid clouds, angels and movement because larger areas of red, blue and pale colour separate the principal bodies. The arrangement directs attention upward without making every figure equally important. Ceremony depends on that hierarchy; otherwise the surrounding activity could overwhelm its central act.

works.title: David Slaying Goliath
works.credit: Peter Paul Rubens. David Slaying Goliath. Image credit: Peter Paul Rubens. Wikimedia Commons. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Resized and JPEG-compressed; selected source frame preserved.
works.description: David’s raised arm and bent body obtain leverage over the fallen giant. At this stage of the story, being smaller does not prevent him from controlling the encounter. The restricted browns concentrate attention on the bodies’ crossing directions, keeping the narrative close to the mechanics of one imminent blow.

works.title: Landscape with an Imaginary View of Tivoli
works.catalogueTitle: Landscape with an Imaginary View of Tivoli
works.credit: Claude Lorrain. Landscape with an Imaginary View of Tivoli. Image credit: Claude Lorrain. Wikimedia Commons. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Resized and JPEG-compressed; selected source frame preserved.
works.description: The title allows the view to be imaginary without making it arbitrary. Bridge, hill, water and foreground shade occupy connected stages, with light giving access to the distance. Claude assembles a coherent place from these relations. Plausible space need not be mistaken for an exact report of topography.

works.title: Portrait of a Man
works.credit: Gerolamo Forabosco. Portrait of a Man. Image credit: Gerolamo Forabosco; Art UK. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Girolamo_Forabosco_(c.1605-1679)_(attributed_to)_-_Portrait_of_a_Man_-_P.1947.LF.133_-_Courtauld_Gallery.jpg. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame resize and JPEG compression; applicable ShareAlike terms retained.
works.description: The fur-trimmed garment occupies an expansive area around a more firmly described face. A pale architectural opening provides a contrasting boundary, while the hand gives the lower part a point of contact. The sitter acquires substance through the relation between likeness and material, without needing an extensive collection of explanatory possessions.

works.title: Saint Lawrence
works.credit: Girolamo da Santacroce. Saint Lawrence. Image credit: Girolamo da Santacroce; Art UK. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Girolamo_da_Santacroce_(1480-1485-1556)_-_Saint_Lawrence_-_P.1947.LF.388_-_Courtauld_Gallery.jpg. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame resize and JPEG compression; applicable ShareAlike terms retained.
works.description: The palm and gridiron identify Lawrence without depicting the violence associated with his martyrdom. His upright figure gathers the attributes into one readable presentation, while angels appear above. The image offers recognition through signs held or displayed beside a person; the story need not be enacted to remain available.

works.title: Saint Sebastian in a Rocky Landscape with Saints Jerome, Anthony Abbot and Christopher
works.catalogueTitle: Saint Sebastian in a Rocky Landscape with Saints Jerome, Anthony Abbot and Christopher
works.credit: Marco Zoppo. Saint Sebastian in a Rocky Landscape with Saints Jerome, Anthony Abbot and Christopher. Image credit: Sailko. Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0). Resized and JPEG-compressed; selected source frame preserved. Additional source attribution: Sailko; Required attribution: I, Sailko. File page: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Marco_zoppo,_san_sebastiano,_1475-78_ca._2.JPG
works.description: Sebastian’s exposed body is larger and more prominent than the other saints distributed through the rocky setting. His raised arm extends its twisting contour. The shared landscape connects a devotional assembly rather than one simultaneous historical incident, allowing differences of scale to indicate how the figures should be attended to.

works.title: A Mandarin Drake
works.credit: Eugène Delacroix. A Mandarin drake. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/eugene-delacroix/a-mandarin-drake
works.description: The plain paper gives the bird’s profile and folded plumage room to remain distinct. Colour divides parts of its construction without dissolving the drake into an ornamental pattern. This close study rewards following how differently marked feathers still belong to one body, rather than assigning the whole image a generalised vividness.

works.title: Boats at Martigues
works.credit: Raoul Dufy. Boats at Martigues. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The hulls crowd together as red, green and blue shapes, with masts rising through the harbour above them. Reflections add another set of adjoining marks. Dufy keeps the boats identifiable while making their relation on the painted surface unusually assertive. The eye can follow vessels and interlocking colour without choosing only one.

works.title: The Colossus of Rhodes
works.credit: Maarten van Heemskerck. Colossus of Rhodes. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/maerten-van-heemskerck/colossus-of-rhodes-1570
works.description: The giant’s legs span a harbour whose ships and people supply measures of its proposed size. Detailed architecture makes the reconstruction persuasive, but does not turn it into an eyewitness record. Heemskerck’s image gives a lost wonder a visible form; the confidence of its drawing should be distinguished from certainty about the ancient monument.

works.title: Cupid and Psyche
works.credit: Joshua Reynolds. Cupid and Psyche. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Psyche’s raised light makes the sleeping Cupid available to her gaze. His body remains unguarded while her leaning posture and lifted arm describe an active search. The mythological encounter turns on unequal awareness, with illumination doing more than modelling flesh: it permits one person to see another who cannot return the look.

works.title: Holy Family with the Infant Saint John and Saint Elizabeth
works.catalogueTitle: Holy Family with the Infant Saint John and Saint Elizabeth
works.credit: Benvenuto Tisi. Holy Family with the Infant Saint John and Saint Elizabeth. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The curtain makes an opening above a tightly assembled group. Inclining adults and children at different heights remain linked through touch rather than arranged as separate frontal figures. Garofalo uses the narrow setting to keep the devotional encounter intimate, while the parted fabric gives that closeness a visible frame.

works.title: Man Holding a Book
works.credit: Rogier van der Weyden. Man holding book. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The open book creates a pale foreground around the hands, while dark headwear and background concentrate the face. Reading supplies an activity without requiring a dramatic gesture. The portrait joins a particular likeness to the careful disposition of fingers and pages, giving stillness enough structure to remain specific.

closingSections.title: Separate access from certainty
paragraphs: Manet’s mirror, Reynolds’s raised light and Bruegel’s small travelling group each determine what a spectator can see. Heemskerck’s reconstruction asks a further question: what does seeing allow us to know? Use the collection records for object details, and current gallery information for display availability; the sequence here is not a confirmed hanging.
